title: Jason Cohen on unfair advantages: adjacency matrix, premium value, and founder role fit
summary: Jason Cohen explains how WP Engine justifies premium pricing through perceived value and authentic culture, and how to evaluate new products with a simple three-level adjacency analysis. He also covers the joy/skill/need test for founder roles, why big decisions get harder at scale, and treating AI as a solution to existing customer problems.

principles.text: Premium pricing works when the customer's perceived value is far above the cost, so make that value specific.
principles.quote: the value they perceive they're getting is 10 times more than that cost even though it's premium that's the question to answer

principles.text: Authentic mission and community can't be bolted on later; they start at day zero and come from who the founder is.
principles.quote: you don't bolt on something that requires being authentic and genuine like that

principles.text: Obsess over brand polish after product-market fit; early on, work out who the customer is and what the product should be.
principles.quote: after product Market fit when things start working it starts to become easy to get customers they're flooding in

principles.text: Good strategy leverages your existing assets and strengths; avoid areas where you're weak unless there's an overwhelming reason.
principles.quote: good strategy leverages those things because that's what you're good at

principles.text: Judge a new product by rating each functional area as trivial, adjustment, or overhaul. No scores, just see the risk and cost.
principles.quote: either you can say it's trivial there's almost no changes required

principles.text: Treat AI as a possible solution to problems customers already have, not as the problem to sell.
principles.quote: it's in the solution space and not the problem space
